content: A pooled bivariate analysis of sensitivity and specificity demonstrated an overall sensitivity of 98% (95% CI: 94–99) and an overall specificity of 99% (95% CI: 97–100). Moderate heterogeneity was observed among the studies included in the bivariate analysis. Fifteen different assays were used for HCV antibody detection, with widely varying cut-offs. Due to the lack of standardized cut-offs, many studies established their own thresholds using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. However, no stratification by test type or cut-off was performed, as this would have resulted in an excessive number of strata, complicating the interpretation of results. Regarding storage conditions, four studies evaluated the impact of different storage conditions on sample integrity. None of the studies left samples at room temperature for more than 24 hours. In a separate pooled analysis, studies were stratified based on whether samples were stored at room temperature for more than 4 hours. This stratification did not significantly alter the high heterogeneity observed in the meta-analysis. In terms of study quality and risk of bias, several studies did not adequately report on key methodological aspects, making it challenging to assess the risk of bias. Four studies employed case-control designs, and only two reported consecutive sampling. While most studies provided some information on sampling, only two blinded laboratory personnel to the reference or index test during testing. Nevertheless, all studies consistently performed both index and reference tests and reported their protocols. Overall, the quality of the studies was graded as moderate. This systematic review and meta-analysis provide moderate-quality evidence supporting the use of dried blood spots (DBS) for HCV antibody testing. The pooled analysis indicates high diagnostic accuracy of DBS samples for detecting HCV antibodies with good precision. Studies assessing agreement between DBS and venous blood testing found strong concordance. Stratification of pooled results by storage conditions revealed only slight differences in sensitivity and specificity for samples stored longer at room temperature. However, as no study reported storage beyond 24 hours, the findings are not generalizable to low-resource settings where prolonged storage may occur. Key limitations of this review include the exclusion of non-English studies and unpublished data, as well as the moderate quality of the included studies. Additionally, the review could not recommend specific commercial tests or cut-offs for DBS-based HCV antibody testing due to the variability in tests used and the lack of individual-level patient data. Future diagnostic accuracy studies should focus on evaluating the applicability of DBS under field transport and storage conditions and report on the cut-offs used with their tests. Manufacturers are encouraged to validate their tests for DBS use, seek regulatory approval for this sample type, and include instructions for DBS testing in their manuals. In conclusion, while the diagnostic accuracy of DBS for HCV antibody testing is high in the studies reviewed, uncertainties regarding optimal storage conditions and cut-offs limit its broader application in low-resource settings. Further research and standardization are needed to address these challenges.
